passages.title: Drying Lumber with Sunlight
passages.text: Freshly sawn boards hold a great deal of water, and a board that dries unevenly will cup, twist or split. A solar kiln solves this cheaply. It is little more than a sloped glazed roof over an insulated box, with a small fan to move air across the stack. Sunlight warms the interior well above the outside temperature, which lets the air carry away more moisture. Vents at each end are opened and closed by hand to control how fast that moisture leaves. The operator's real skill lies in restraint. Pushing the wood too hard in the first week drives water out of the surface faster than it can travel from the core, and the outer shell sets hard while the inside is still wet. Boards treated this way look fine until they are cut, when the trapped stress releases and the piece bows. Patient operators dry slowly at first and accept that a load may take two months rather than three weeks.

passages.title: Colours on the Flight Deck
passages.text: An aircraft carrier deck during flight operations is one of the noisiest workplaces anywhere, and spoken instructions are largely useless. The crew solves this with colour. Each person wears a jersey whose colour announces a job: fuel handlers in purple, ordnance in red, catapult and arresting gear crews in green, aircraft directors in yellow, and maintenance in brown. A sailor glancing across the deck can tell at once who is authorised to be where, and more importantly who is not. The system also works in reverse. A pilot taxiing forward follows the hand signals of a yellow shirt alone, and ignores every other gesture on the deck, however urgent it looks. That single rule prevents the confusion that would follow if several people could direct the same aircraft. Colour coding costs nothing, survives the noise, and works at a distance where a voice would be lost entirely.

passages.title: The Lighthouse Lens
passages.text: Before the nineteenth century a lighthouse was mostly a large fire behind glass, and most of its light escaped uselessly into the sky and the ground. The Fresnel lens changed that. Instead of one thick curved piece of glass, which would have been impossibly heavy, the design uses a series of concentric rings, each ground at its own angle. Together the rings bend light that would have scattered into a single flat beam aimed at the horizon. The saving is dramatic: a lens of this kind can send a useful beam more than twenty miles out to sea using a modest oil lamp. The rings also made the lens light enough to float on a bath of mercury, so a keeper could set the whole assembly turning with a gentle push. What a sailor saw as a flashing signal was simply that rotation carrying the beam past the ship.

passages.title: Inspecting a Pipeline from Inside
passages.text: A buried pipeline cannot be examined from outside without digging it up, so operators send a device through the inside instead. These tools are called pigs, and the simplest kind is little more than a plug pushed along by the product in the line, scraping wax and debris off the wall as it goes. The more capable versions carry instruments. A magnetic pig records places where the steel has thinned, which is usually the first sign of corrosion. An ultrasonic pig measures wall thickness directly and to finer tolerances, though it needs liquid around it to work and so cannot be used in a gas line. The readings are stored on board and read out when the pig is recovered at the far end. Because the line keeps flowing throughout, an operator can survey many miles of pipe without shutting anything down, which is the main reason the method has spread.

passages.title: Dust in the Grain Elevator
passages.text: Grain looks inert, but the fine dust it sheds is not. Suspended in air at the right concentration, that dust burns almost instantly when it meets a spark, and the pressure wave from the first ignition throws settled dust off every beam and ledge into the air, where it feeds a second and far larger explosion. The secondary blast does most of the damage. This is why housekeeping in an elevator is treated as a safety task rather than a cosmetic one. Crews sweep ledges that no visitor would ever see, and designers avoid flat horizontal surfaces wherever a sloped one will do. Equipment is bonded and grounded so that static cannot build, and bearings are monitored for heat because a bearing running hot is a spark waiting to happen. None of these measures is dramatic. Together they keep the first ignition from occurring at all, which is the only reliable way to prevent the second.

passages.title: Keeping a Hive Cool
passages.text: A honeybee colony holds its brood nest close to ninety-five degrees whatever the weather outside, and in midsummer the problem is shedding heat rather than making it. The bees solve it with water and moving air. Foragers bring water back and spread it in thin films across the comb, and other bees stand at the entrance fanning with their wings to draw a current through the hive. Evaporation from those films carries heat away, much as sweat cools skin. The arrangement is surprisingly precise: fanning bees position themselves so that air enters at one side of the entrance and leaves at the other, rather than each bee blowing in whatever direction it happens to face. A beekeeper who narrows the entrance in hot weather, meaning to keep robbers out, can defeat this system entirely and cook the colony.

passages.title: Bringing Down the Snow on Purpose
passages.text: Ski patrols and highway crews do not wait for an unstable slope to release on its own. They trigger it, usually early in the morning before anyone is beneath it. Crews therefore work in bad weather rather than waiting for it to clear, which is the opposite of what most outdoor work requires.

passages.title: How a Canal Lock Works
passages.text: A canal that crosses rising ground cannot simply slope upward, because water would run down it. Instead the route is cut into level reaches joined by locks, and a lock is nothing more than a chamber with a gate at each end. A boat travelling uphill enters through the lower gate, which closes behind it. Valves then admit water from the reach above until the level inside the chamber matches the level ahead, at which point the upper gate can be opened and the boat moves on, several feet higher than it started. Going downhill the sequence runs in reverse and water is let out instead. No pumps are involved anywhere. Every lockful drains downhill under gravity, which means a busy flight of locks slowly empties the summit reach, and canals are built with reservoirs to make that loss good.

passages.title: Strengthening an Old Building
passages.text: Buildings put up before modern codes often stand on the wrong principle for an earthquake. passages.title: Training Under Water
passages.text: Weightlessness cannot be produced on the ground for more than a few seconds, so astronauts rehearse spacewalks in a pool deep enough to hold a full-size mockup of the spacecraft. A suited crew member is weighted until they neither rise nor sink, a condition called neutral buoyancy, and can then be positioned anywhere around the structure as if floating. The simulation is good enough to learn a procedure and to find out that a handhold is in the wrong place, which is its real purpose. It is not the same as weightlessness. Water resists movement, so a trainee who pushes off drifts to a stop instead of continuing, and the suit still hangs on the body in a way it will not in orbit. passages.title: Storing Water in a Stem
passages.text: A desert plant faces two problems at once: rain arrives rarely and in quantity, and water is lost whenever the pores in a leaf open to admit the air a plant needs. A cactus answers both by changing what its parts do. The stem takes over photosynthesis and swells to store water, its pleated surface letting it expand without splitting, while the leaves are reduced to spines that shade the surface and lose almost nothing. The pores themselves open at night rather than by day, taking in air when the surrounding air is cool and damp, and storing the result chemically until sunlight is available. Each of these changes costs the plant something in growth rate, which is why a cactus grows slowly even in a good year and why damage to one is slow to repair.

passages.title: Breaking a Channel
passages.text: An icebreaker does not push through ice so much as climb onto it. The bow is shaped so the hull rides up over the edge of the sheet, and the ship's weight then cracks the ice beneath, after which the broken pieces are pushed aside by the flaring hull. In thick ice a ship may back up and ram repeatedly, gaining a length at a time. passages.title: Small Whirlwinds
passages.text: A dust devil is not a small tornado, despite the resemblance, and the difference is in where it starts. A tornado descends from a storm cloud; a dust devil begins at the ground on a clear day. Sun heats a patch of bare earth far above the temperature of the air around it, and that superheated air breaks away and rises through the cooler air above. Air rushing in underneath to replace it acquires a spin from whatever small rotation the surface flow already had, and the column tightens and speeds up as it stretches upward, in the same way a spinning skater draws in their arms. The dust is incidental, picked up and made visible by a vortex that was already there. This is why dust devils are common on dry ground and almost unknown over a lawn.
